s: God has will (governing the birth of the Sage)
q: The birth of the Sage is the will of God; his death is but a modification of existence.

s: God possesses TÊ (shared by the Sage in repose)
q: Thus unconditioned and in repose, he is a partaker of the virtue of God."

s: spirituality is a pure and simple state (preserved by the Tao of the pure and simple)
q: The TAO of the pure and simple consists in preserving spirituality.

s: spirituality operates freely unity with itself (after being preserved and united with itself)
q: He who preserves his spirituality and loses it not, becomes one with that spirituality. And through that unity the spirit operates freely, and comes into due relationship with God.

s: spirituality comes into relationship with God (through unity with itself)
q: And through that unity the spirit operates freely, and comes into due relationship with God.

s: self-conceit is affected by recluses (as a form of personal over-estimation)
q: Self-conceit and assurance, which lead men to quit society, and be different from their fellows, to indulge in tall talk and abuse of others,--these are nothing more than personal over-estimation, the affectation of recluses and those who have done with the world and have closed their hearts to mundane influences.

s: soul is valued by Sages of old (more than money, fame, or resolution)
q: A vulgar saying has it, "The masses value money; honest men, fame; virtuous men, resolution; and Sages, the soul."

s: TÊ is a perfect state (when the heart is unconscious of sorrow and happiness)
q: The heart unconscious of sorrow and happiness,--that is perfect virtue.

s: TÊ is lost through love (love and hate cause its loss)
q: Sorrow and happiness are the heresies Evil influences. of virtue; joy and anger lead astray from TAO; love and hate cause the loss of virtue

s: passivity produces repose (in the Sage)
q: Being passive he is in a state of repose.

s: passivity prevents sorrow (when joined with repose)
q: Being passive he is in a state of repose. And where passivity and repose are, there sorrow and anxiety do not enter, and foul influences do not collect.

s: repose prevents anxiety (when joined with passivity)
q: Being passive he is in a state of repose. And where passivity and repose are, there sorrow and anxiety do not enter, and foul influences do not collect.

s: repose is a perfect state (when it is one and without change)
q: ONE, without change,--that is perfect repose.

s: THE UNIVERSE has TAO (as its way and constitution)
q: Such is the TAO of the universe, such is the virtue of the Sage.

s: Chapter XV is titled self-conceit
q: CHAPTER XV. SELF-CONCEIT.

s: Sages of old is a negative quantity (and therefore passive)
q: Wherefore it has been said, "The Sage is a negative quantity, and is consequently in a state of passivity.

s: Sages of old possesses TÊ (complete through passivity and repose)
q: And thus his virtue is complete and his spirituality unimpaired.

s: Sages of old possesses spirituality (unimpaired)
q: And thus his virtue is complete and his spirituality unimpaired.

s: Sages of old shares passivity (in repose, with the Yin)
q: In repose, he shares the passivity of the _Yin_; in action, the energy of the _Yang_.

s: Sages of old has no anxieties (as one resigned to the laws of God)
q: He floats through life to rest in death. He has no anxieties; he makes no plans.

s: Sages of old has dreamless sleep (as part of pure spirituality)
q: His sleep is dreamless, his awaking without pain. His spirituality is pure,

s: TAO is a order
q: Virtue is harmony; TAO is order.

s: the world destroys TAO (mutually)
q: Thus it may be said that the world destroys TAO

s: the world is destroyed by TAO (mutually)
q: and that TAO destroys the world.

s: the Empire is plunged into confusion (when music and ceremonial are ill regulated)
q: If music and ceremonial are ill regulated, the empire is plunged into confusion.

s: the Empire is ruled by Sui Jen
q: Sui Jen The Prometheus of China. and Fu Hsi See ch. vi. ruled the empire.

s: the Empire is ruled by Fu Hsi
q: Sui Jen The Prometheus of China. and Fu Hsi See ch. vi. ruled the empire.

s: the Empire is ruled by Shên Nung
q: Shên Nung The inventor of agriculture. and Huang Ti The Yellow Emperor. See ch. vi. ruled the empire.

s: the Empire is ruled by Yellow Emperor
q: Shên Nung The inventor of agriculture. and Huang Ti The Yellow Emperor. See ch. vi. ruled the empire.

s: the Empire is ruled by Yao
q: Yao and Shun ruled the empire.

s: the Empire is ruled by Shun
q: Yao and Shun ruled the empire.

s: primeval man enjoys perfect tranquillity (throughout life)
q: Primeval man enjoyed perfect tranquillity throughout life.

s: TAO is unattainable through mundane arts
q: TAO unattainable by mundane arts

s: primeval man has Wisdom (without occasion to use it)
q: men had knowledge, but no occasion to use it.

s: man loses original integrity (under systems of government and moral reform)
q: Systems of government and moral reform were introduced. Man's original integrity was scattered.

s: man discards natural instincts
q: Then he discarded natural instinct and took up with the intellectual.

s: man takes up intellectual
q: Then he discarded natural instinct and took up with the intellectual.

s: man is unable to revert to natural instincts (after confusion sets in)
q: man was unable to revert to his natural instincts, to the condition in which he at first existed.

s: the ancients cultivate TAO
q: The ancients, in cultivating TAO, begat knowledge out of repose.

s: Wisdom is begotten out of repose (by the ancients)
q: The ancients, in cultivating TAO, begat knowledge out of repose.

s: Wisdom produces repose (mutually)
q: Knowledge and repose thus mutually producing each other, harmony and order were developed.

s: repose produces Wisdom (mutually)
q: Knowledge and repose thus mutually producing each other, harmony and order were developed.

s: TAO is destroyed by the world
q: Thus it may be said that the world destroys TAO

s: government is introduced the world (as virtue declines)
q: Again virtue declined. Yao and Shun ruled the empire. Systems of government and moral reform were introduced.

s: natural instincts is discarded by man
q: Then he discarded natural instinct and took up with the intellectual.

s: natural instincts is lost through worldliness
q: Those who over-estimate the external and lose their natural instincts in worldliness,--these are the people of topsy-turvydom.

s: Sages of old have virtue (hidden even when not dwelling on mountain and in forest)
q: Though the Sages were not to dwell on mountain and in forest, their virtue would still be hidden;--hidden, but not by themselves.

s: retired scholars are not men who hid their bodies, or kept back their words, or concealed their wisdom
q: Those of old who were called retired scholars, were not men who hid their bodies, or kept back their words, or concealed their wisdom.

s: retired scholars preserve themselves (when the age is unsuitable and their mission fails)
q: If the age was unsuitable and their mission at failure, they fell back upon their own resources and waited. Such is the way to preserve oneself.

s: office is external (not a part of oneself)
q: It meant that nothing could be added to the sum of happiness. But now it does mean office, though office is external and is not a part of oneself.

s: office causes unhappiness (in the present age)
q: But now-a-days, both having and not having Office. are causes of unhappiness.

s: happiness is complete (when desire is attained)
q: He whose happiness is complete has attained his desire.

s: happiness is not exempt from sorrow
q: From which we may infer that even happiness is not exempt from sorrow.

s: TAO destroys the world (mutually)
q: and that TAO destroys the world.

s: Positive and Negative principles are peacefully united (in primeval man's day)
q: In his day, the Positive and Negative principles were peacefully united

s: death is unknown (in primeval man's day)
q: death was unknown

s: charity springs from TÊ
q: Virtue all-embracing,--hence charity.

s: duty to one's neighbour springs from TAO (through TAO's influence on all)
q: TAO all-influencing,--hence duty to one's neighbour.

s: loyalty springs from charity (after the establishment of charity and duty to one's neighbour)
q: From the establishment of these two springs loyalty.

s: ceremonial expresses sincerity (in ornamental guise)
q: followed by ceremonial, or sincerity expressed in ornamental guise.

s: TAO does not deal with detail
q: TAO does not deal with detail.

s: Yellow Emperor is a Yellow Emperor
q: Huang Ti The Yellow Emperor. See ch. vi.

s: TÊ is a harmony
q: Virtue is harmony; TAO is order.

s: TÊ is all-embracing
q: Virtue all-embracing,--hence charity.

s: TÊ declines through historical ages
q: By and by, virtue declined.

s: TÊ is injured by trifles
q: Trifles injure virtue; detail injures TAO.

s: autumn floods is a seasonal flooding
q: It was the time of autumn floods.

s: ocean is never empty (despite constant drainage)
q: It is constantly being drained off, yet it is never empty.

s: ocean gets its shape from THE UNIVERSE
q: for I get my shape from the universe, my vital power from the _Yin_ and _Yang_.

s: ocean is small relative to the universe (as a stone or tree on a vast mountain)
q: In the universe I am but as a small stone or a small tree on a vast mountain.

s: TAO is a the only absolute (unconditioned)
q: The only absolute is TAO

s: TAO has no beginning
q: TAO is without beginning, without end.

s: TAO has no end
q: TAO is without beginning, without end.

s: TAO is unconditioned (embracing all creation)
q: Embrace all creation, and none shall be more sheltered than another. This is the unconditioned.

s: TAO determines greatness and smallness (through relativity)
q: If we say that a thing is great or small because it is relatively great or small, then there is nothing in all creation which is not great, nothing which is not small.

s: TAO contains no value and worthlessness extremes (from its point of view)
q: From the point of view of TAO," replied the Spirit of the Ocean, "there are no such extremes of value or worthlessness.

s: river receives streams (during autumn floods)
q: Every stream poured into the river, which swelled in its turbid course.

s: THE UNIVERSE contains Four Seas (as puddles in a marsh)
q: The Four Seas,--are they not to the universe but like puddles in a marsh?

s: Time is endless
q: Dimensions are limitless; time is endless.

s: great Space is infinite
q: Thus, the wise man looks into space, and does not regard the small as too little, nor the great as too much; for he knows that there is no limit to dimension.

s: dimensions are limitless
q: Dimensions are limitless; time is endless.

s: greatness and smallness are relative (not absolute)
q: If we say that a thing is great or small because it is relatively great or small, then there is nothing in all creation which is not great, nothing which is not small.

s: value and worthlessness are relative (from the point of view of TAO)
q: From the point of view of TAO," replied the Spirit of the Ocean, "there are no such extremes of value or worthlessness.

s: man of TAO has no reputation
q: I have heard say, the man of TAO has no reputation; perfect virtue acquires nothing; the truly great man ignores self;--this is the height of self-discipline.

s: river has turbid course (during autumn floods)
q: Every stream poured into the river, which swelled in its turbid course.

s: truly virtuous man ignores self (as self-discipline)
q: the truly great man ignores self;--this is the height of self-discipline.

s: truly virtuous man does not credit himself with charity and mercy (although he does not injure others)
q: Therefore, the truly great man, although he does not injure others, does not credit himself with charity and mercy.

s: Perfect Man is unharmed by fire, water, frost, sun, wild birds, and wild beasts (through discrimination between safety and danger)
q: The man of perfect virtue cannot be burnt by fire, nor drowned in water, nor hurt by frost or sun, nor torn by wild bird or beast.

s: Perfect Man discriminates between safety and danger
q: Not that he makes light of these; but that he discriminates between safety and danger.

s: the natural is a inner principle (abiding within)
q: Therefore it has been said that the natural abides within, the artificial without. Virtue abides in the natural.

s: artificial is a external condition (abiding without)
q: Therefore it has been said that the natural abides within, the artificial without. Virtue abides in the natural.

s: TÊ abides in the natural
q: Virtue abides in the natural.

s: horses have four feet (naturally)
q: Horses and oxen," answered the Spirit of the Ocean, "have four feet. That is the natural.

s: Spirit of the River is a spirit of a river
q: Then the Spirit of the River laughed for joy that all the beauty of the earth was gathered to himself.

s: Confucius is associated with learning (people detract from it or underrate it)
q: When formerly I heard people detracting from the learning of Confucius or underrating the heroism of Poh I,
